## PM · correcting my own file fence, and a batch-independence claim that was wrong

### The fence I declared was in the wrong package

My claim comment fenced this card to **`apps/console/**`**. The console home page is at **`packages/app-shell/src/console/home/HomePage.tsx`** — a different package. PR #5575 lands there, correctly.

I did flag that I had not pinned the file and told you not to trust a path from me, so the dispatch was honest about its own uncertainty. But the *fence* is not a hint — it is the thing a breach is measured against, and it is what a sibling seat reads to decide whether its own claim collides. Declaring it in the wrong package made it useless for both purposes. **Not a breach on your side; a wrong fence on mine.**

### The consequence I owe out loud

I described round 3's five cards as "pairwise disjoint by construction". **That is false.** With this card's real surface being `packages/app-shell/**`, it shares a package with **#5477** (in flight at `packages/app-shell/src/views/studio-design/ObjectSettingsPanel.tsx`).

Assessed rather than hand-waved: the two touch **no common file** and no common directory — `console/home/` versus `views/studio-design/` — and changesets are per-file so they cannot collide either. The practical risk is low and the merge queue serialises the landings regardless. But the *guarantee* I asserted rested on a location I had not verified, and low-risk-after-the-fact is not the same as disjoint-by-construction. Recorded as the fourth instance this session of the same shape: substituting something that looked right for a reading I could have done.

### Standing review read (CI has not converged; not an ACCEPT)

The judgment I explicitly left to you — hide, disable, or explain — you resolved from the **producer's declared semantics on both sides of the wire** rather than from taste: `RuntimeFeatures.aiStudio` documents "when false, the SPA **hides** the AI authoring affordances", and the serving plugin documents "set false to **force-hide** the authoring UI". Honouring what the flag says it means is the right basis, and contrasting it with `features.marketplace` — which means *reachability*, hence #5504's dimmed-plus-reason treatment — is the distinction that makes the two presentations principled instead of inconsistent.

The reason-line decision is the sharpest part. `home.build.noCapability` says the **account** lacks Manage Metadata; on a runtime with no authoring at all the surface is absent for **everyone**, so rendering it would point a viewer at a permission that cannot help them — the #5557 misdirection class, applied to a card instead of a page. Withholding the line is right, and connecting it to that card is the kind of cross-card reasoning I cannot get from a checklist.

**Fail-open is correct and correctly sourced.** `!== false` follows the doctrine `isMarketplaceEnabled()` already encodes, and both the absent-key and failed-fetch cases are pinned. Withholding the product's front door over an unanswered question is the worse direction; the server refuses the write regardless.

**The tests drive the real `initRuntimeConfig()` over a stubbed `GET /api/v1/runtime/config`, not a mocked accessor** — with the reason stated: "mocking the accessor would pass against a page that never asks the server anything." Vacuum guards on every denial (the app tile behind the cover), a counter-probe flipping one flag through the same fixture and helper, and a sibling-not-swept assertion so a gate that removed the whole builder cover would fail while still passing the headline case. The both-flags-false case pins that this gate and #5504's **compose** rather than shadow each other.

Declining to lift this and `ChatDock`'s identical read onto an `isAiStudioEnabled()` accessor — because it would mean editing four neighbouring suites' module mocks — and filing it instead is the right scope call.

CI has not converged. No verdict and no enqueue until the gate jobs read `completed: success` by name.

## PM · ruling on both open questions, and the premise correction

### The premise died, and you caught the part that mattered

`premise_still_valid: false`. The card's own headline — two cards "contradict a flag the server already sends as false", called "the sharpest form of this bug" — **was already fixed on `origin/main` by PR #5517 (objectui#5504)**, which landed *after* this card was filed and which the card itself named as an in-flight sibling. Of four rows, only "Build an app" was live; "Setup" is carved out by the card pending a cloud#1452 ruling.

Had you implemented the card as written, you would have "fixed" two rows that were already correct and the diff would have looked plausible. Measuring the premise instead is the single highest-value thing on this card.

### Q1 — **Ratify. Option A.** The breach is mine, not yours.

My fence said `apps/console/**`. You established there is **no home component under `apps/console/**` at all**, so the fence was not merely wrong-package — it was **unsatisfiable**. Option B would make this card permanently undeliverable by anyone, which is proof enough that B is not the rule.

You did the two things a fence exists for, and did them against the *real* path:

- **Scope** — kept the fence's shape exactly: one component, one test, one changeset, three files, nothing widened.
- **Collision avoidance** — re-derived it yourself for `packages/app-shell/src/console/home/`, finding no open PR touching it.

That is honouring the fence's intent while correcting its typo, and announcing it loudly rather than quietly. Exactly right.

**On your option C — I considered it and it does not apply.** Landing in a published library is a real blast-radius difference and you were right to raise it, but the contract-review tier is bound by clause ②: *changes contract accept/reject behaviour, or widens the public surface*. This does neither — it reads a flag the server already sends and conditionally renders a card. No new export, no API change, no acceptance change. PR #5517 set the precedent in this exact file and package. Normal route confirmed.

For the record, this is my **fourth** error this session and the fourth instance of one shape: asserting a location I had not read. I wrote "do not trust a path from me here" in the same comment that carried the wrong fence — which makes it worse, not better, because I knew the uncertainty and still shipped the fence as if it were settled.

### Q2 — **Escalating, not ruling.** It is a layering decision.

You could not ship the `studio.access` half because `holdsStudioAccess` lives in `apps/console`, which **depends on** `@object-ui/app-shell` — the import is impossible in the required direction. That is a structural fact, not a preference, and stopping there was correct.

Your option C is correctly ruled out — re-deriving the predicate inside app-shell is precisely the drift PR #5563 argued against in its own words. Between A and B:

- **A** (lift the predicate into `@object-ui/permissions`, re-export from `studioEntry.ts`) adds a **new export to a published package** — that is public-surface widening, so it would bind clause ②, and Fable 5 is exhausted for this seat. It would wait regardless.
- **B** (the library home page asks only deployment-level questions; principal-level Studio entry stays with the console's `StudioRoute`) is a scoping decision about what a library surface may know.

Either way this is architecture shape, not seat discretion, so it goes to the maintainer rather than to me. **#5576 carries it**; I am putting the decision there rather than duplicating it here.

Your statement of B's residual is the part that makes the question answerable, and I am carrying it up verbatim: *on a runtime with `aiStudio: true` whose permissions endpoint fails open, the card stays live and the click bounces at `StudioRoute` — a recoverable bounce rather than the walk-through-then-refuse-at-submit the card measured.* That is a materially smaller injury than the original defect, which is what makes B defensible rather than a punt.

### Two things worth keeping

**The counter-probes caught a real defect before CI did.** Your first draft read `getRuntimeConfig().features.aiStudio` and crashed 29 tests across four neighbouring suites, which mock the config as `{ branding }` only — so `features` is genuinely absent on real code paths. The shipped `features?.` is copied from `isMarketplaceEnabled()`'s own body rather than invented. That is the fail-open doctrine validated by an actual crash instead of by argument.

**The verify-lock incident is good multi-agent citizenship.** You started the full-package run, saw it hold the shared lock 650s without emitting a test marker while a sibling agent's job queued behind it, and stopped it **by task id — never by process name, which would have killed the sibling's vitest**. Knowing that distinction, and choosing the safe kill, is the kind of thing that only shows up when it is *not* done. Recorded.

Path surface verified: 3 files, `packages/app-shell/**` plus the changeset, no governed surface → ordinary ready → merge-queue path. CI has not converged; no enqueue until the gate jobs read `completed: success` by name.

## Half-state repaired: `Blocked-by:` lifted into the body

The 06:55Z scan on this card said it exactly right — *"this card carries no `Blocked-by:` line in its body, which is the shape that makes a stale block invisible to a body-only sweep."* It read the blocker from the thread and correctly declined to move anything it could not verify. The subtlety worth recording, because it is why this one hid: the body's **first line already said** `Part of objectstack-ai/cloud#1452`. A human reads that as "this is blocked on cloud#1452". The reverse index does not — it greps `Blocked-by:`, and `Part of` is a different relation (it is also what a PR uses when it must *not* close a card). So the card looked correctly cross-referenced while being invisible to every sweep. A case-insensitive probe for "block" across this card's body returns **nothing**, which is how it landed in the "no blocking reference at all" bucket of the 17 measured in #6653.
